# Numbers

A bare number such as `0.5` is approximate: a float of the default width: 64 bits under dynamic kinds and 32 under static kinds, unless [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) sets a width. A number marked with `ₓ`, such as `3ₓ`, is an ordinary integer, exact under the default dynamic kinds. `1r3` is an exact rational. A byte-count suffix such as `ₓ₄` selects a fixed-width integer. Comparisons give Booleans, written `$t` and `$f`.

## Writing numbers

| Written | Value |
|---|---|
| `3`, `0.5`, `1E¯3`, `1ₑ¯3` | Approximate numbers. `e`, `E` or `ₑ` writes an exponent |
| `¯2` | A negative number. [`¯`](glyphs/overbar.qmd) is part of the number, and [`-`](glyphs/minus.qmd) is a function |
| `3ₓ` | An exact integer |
| `3ₓ₁`, `3ₓ₂`, `3ₓ₄`, `3ₓ₈` | A fixed-width integer occupying 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes |
| `1r3`, `1ᵣ3` | An exact rational |
| `2j3`, `2J3`, `2ⱼ3` | A complex number, 2 + 3i, with approximate parts |
| `∞`, `¯∞` | [Infinities](glyphs/infinity.qmd) |
| `$n` | NaN |
| `$t`, `$f` | True and false |
| `1.5ₕ`, `1.5ₛ`, `1.5ₚ` | A 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, whatever the default width |
| `2j3ₛ`, `2j3ₚ` | A complex number with 32-bit or 64-bit parts. `2j3ₕ` has 32-bit parts too |
| `⍬`, `⍬ₓ`, `⍬ₕ`, `⍬ₛ`, `⍬ₚ` | The approximate, the exact, and the 16-bit, 32-bit and 64-bit [empty vector](glyphs/zilde.qmd) |
| `[…]ₓ`, `(…)ₓ` | A list, or rows, in which every number is exact |
| `[…]ₕ`, `[…]ₛ`, `[…]ₚ` | A list, or rows, in which every real number is a 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, and every complex number has parts of that width, or 32-bit parts after `ₕ` |
| `xⱼy`, `xₑy`, `xᵣy` | Between two items, such as names: `x+y×0ⱼ1`, `x×10*y` and the exact quotient of `xₓ` by `yₓ`, as one term |

A plain `e`, `j` or `r` starts a name unless the rest of a number follows it, as in `1e5`, `1r3` and `2j3`. Results display with the subscript forms, as in `1ᵣ3`, `2ⱼ3` and `1ₑ20`. A subscript form that the rest of a number doesn't follow, or one between two other items such as names, joins the items on each side into one term, as a literal is one, with the value the table gives. A literal on the left gives what the all-literal form gives: with `n←3`, `2ₑn` is `2ₑ3`.

```bpl
1j2+3j4              ⍝ 4j6
1E¯3                 ⍝ 0.001
¯2+5                 ⍝ 3
2J3≡2j3              ⍝ $t
1ᵣ3≡1r3              ⍝ $t
edges←3 ⋄ 2edges     ⍝ 2 3
x←2 ⋄ n←3 ⋄ xⱼn      ⍝ 2j3
2ₑn                  ⍝ 2000
```

## Exact and approximate

Exact arithmetic grows as needed. Mixing exact and approximate numbers gives an approximate result. Examples on these pages write `ₓ` for exact input.

```bpl
1÷3                  ⍝ 0.3333333333333333
1ₓ÷3ₓ                ⍝ 1r3
1r3+1r6              ⍝ 1r2
1r2+0.5              ⍝ 1
9223372036854775807ₓ+1ₓ ⍝ 9223372036854775808ₓ
```

A function keeps exact integers exact only if every finite result it gives for them is rational. Arithmetic, `!`, and `*` with an integer exponent keep them exact. `√`, `⍟`, `π`, `○` and monadic `*` give approximate results, whole ones included. An exact function gives the float `∞` at a pole, such as `÷0ₓ`:

```bpl
2ₓ*¯2ₓ               ⍝ 1r4
!20ₓ                 ⍝ 2432902008176640000ₓ
√4ₓ                  ⍝ 2
÷0ₓ                  ⍝ ∞
```

Predicates, positions, tally, shape, and monadic `⌊`, `⌈` and `×` return exact integers. A float beyond the `i64` range floors to an exact big integer:

```bpl
⌊2.5 ¯2.5            ⍝ [2 ¯3]ₓ
⌊2*70                ⍝ 1180591620717411303424ₓ
```

Iota and random integer generation keep an exact argument exact. An argument that must be a whole number, such as an index or a count, accepts a float within `1E¯14` of one, whatever the [`mathish` setting](system/prefs.qmd):

```bpl
⍳10×0.1×3          ⍝ 0 1 2
```

## Numbers in one array

Numbers that an operation puts in one array share a kind. A float among exact integers makes them all floats, and a complex number makes every number complex:

```bpl
⍳3ₓ , 0.5            ⍝ 0 1 2 0.5
⍳2ₓ , 1j2            ⍝ 0 1 1j2
1ₓ,0.5 ÷ 2ₓ          ⍝ 0.5 0.25
```

Each number written in a literal list or in brackets keeps its own exactness, even beside numbers of the other kind. Floats written beside complex numbers become complex. Their values don't change:

```bpl
1ₓ 0.5÷2ₓ            ⍝ 1r2 0.25
[1ₓ 0.5]÷2ₓ          ⍝ 1r2 0.25
```

Under dynamic kinds, a write keeps each number's exactness too. A float assigned among exact integers, or an exact integer among floats, leaves the array mixed, however the array was made. A Boolean written among other numbers, or a number written among Booleans, leaves it mixed in the same way. Under static kinds, the whole array takes the compact type that holds both its items and the items written, as catenating them would: a float written among bytes makes the array floats. Only items that no compact type holds, such as characters among numbers, leave it mixed. Mixed storage is slower. To keep an array compact, write values of its own kind, as the [style guide](style.qmd) shows. [`•explain`](system/explain.qmd) lists each write that left an array mixed, in its `mixed` record. To give an existing array one kind, convert it: `⌊` makes exact integers, `×1` makes floats, and `+0ₓ` compacts items that already share a kind:

```bpl
r←["a":2ₓ "b":3ₓ]
r.b←2.5
r                    ⍝ ["a":2ₓ "b":2.5]
m←3⍴$f
m.[[1]]←1
m                    ⍝ $f 1 $f
```

Around literals, `[…]ₓ` and `(…)ₓ` make every number exact, at any depth. Each number must be whole. After a list or group that holds anything else, as after a name, `ₓ` floors to exact integers, as [Superscripts and subscripts](scripts.ipynb) describes. A vector of exact integers displays as `[…]ₓ`, and rows of them as `(…)ₓ`. `⍕` writes them the same way:

```bpl
[1 0 1]ₓ≡1ₓ 0ₓ 1ₓ    ⍝ $t
[[1 2] 3]ₓ≡[1ₓ 2ₓ;3ₓ]   ⍝ $t
(0 1⋄2 3)ₓ≡[[0 1]ₓ [2 3]ₓ]  ⍝ $t
1↑⍬ₓ                 ⍝ [0]ₓ
⍕1ₓ ¯2ₓ              ⍝ "[1 ¯2]ₓ"
```

## Weak and strong numbers

An ordinary integer literal such as `1ₓ`, or an unmarked float or complex literal, is weak. Python `int`, `float` and `complex` arguments are weak too. Arithmetic on weak values gives weak ordinary results. A strong operand makes the ordinary result strong.

An explicit float-width literal or a fixed-width integer is strong. So is a number read by `•json` or `•csv`. Constructing an array makes its items strong. Selecting an item preserves that strength.

## Storage

`(•storage x).kind` names an array's storage kind. Ordinary integers report `integer` regardless of their byte width. Fixed-width integers report their type, such as `uint8` for `ₓ₁`. Mixed storage keeps each item's own kind. A literal list of exact and approximate numbers uses it:

```bpl
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage x).kind      ⍝ "mixed"
```

Rationals and exact integers beyond 64 bits have no compact storage. An array that holds one uses mixed storage, as does an array that holds numbers together with characters, nested arrays or functions. A JSON object or a Python dict reads as a literal of its fields does, so its storage is mixed only where the fields need it.

Selecting from, catenating or assigning into mixed storage keeps each item's kind. A selection or catenation whose items one compact storage holds uses it, as the same items written in brackets do: `1↓'a' 1ₓ 2ₓ` is held as integers. An assignment into mixed storage leaves it mixed. Arithmetic builds fresh storage from its results, and each result keeps its own kind. Every result of `1×x` is approximate, which makes it a float array. `1ₓ×x` keeps the exact results exact:

```bpl
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage 1×x).kind    ⍝ "float64"
(•storage 1ₓ×x).kind   ⍝ "mixed"
```

Display depends on an array's items, not on how they're stored. Boxed display marks an array whose items differ in kind with `+`, and one whose items are all exact integers with `ₓ`, whichever storage holds them.

Ordinary integer storage keeps each item in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. One byte holds 0 to 255. Literals, reductions and positions take the fewest bytes that hold every item. Pervasive arithmetic keeps its arguments' size, and moves to the next size up when a result doesn't fit. An exact result beyond 8 bytes becomes a big integer in mixed storage. The size never changes an ordinary result, and `•storage` doesn't show it. Imported typed integer buffers use the fixed-width rules below.

## Fixed-width integers

The suffix gives a number of bytes. `ₓ₁` selects unsigned `u8`; `ₓ₂`, `ₓ₄` and `ₓ₈` select signed `i16`, `i32` and `i64`. The width stays with a value through selection, rebuilding and arithmetic. Integer results wrap at their selected width rather than growing. The `int` preference does not override an explicit fixed width.

```bpl
255ₓ₁+1ₓ            ⍝ 0ₓ₁
255ₓ₁+↑[1]ₓ         ⍝ 256ₓ
32767ₓ₂+1ₓ          ⍝ ¯32768ₓ₂
200ₓ₁∧199ₓ₁         ⍝ 120ₓ₁
[200 100]ₓ₁<300ₓ     ⍝ $t $t
```

Two fixed integers compute at the wider type. In arithmetic, catenation, union and writes, a [weak ordinary integer](#weak-and-strong-numbers) takes the fixed type if it fits, and raises otherwise. A strong ordinary integer makes the result ordinary, under the current `kinds` setting. Booleans take the fixed type too. Floats follow their existing promotion rules. True division gives 32-bit floats for `u8` and `i16`, and 64-bit floats for `i32` and `i64`, no wider than the `float` preference. Under static kinds, where the default is 32 bits, `i32` and `i64` divide to 32-bit floats too. Comparisons give Booleans without requiring a weak argument to fit the fixed type.

Functions that rearrange or select items keep the fixed type, as sort and `↑` do. So do functions whose results can't exceed a fixed argument: `⍳`, `↦`, roll, deal, `⊤` and monadic `⨸`. Functions built from `+`, `-` and `×` compute at the fixed type and wrap, as `+/` does. These are `⊥`, polynomial evaluation with `⌻`, `!`, the determinant `-.×` and the permanent `+.×`. A result of `∧`, `∨` or `!` that doesn't fit the fixed type wraps, as a sum does. Positions, counts and values that can exceed the argument's range are ordinary integers, such as the results of `⍸`, `⍋`, `≢` and `⍭`. A function with no kernel at the fixed width gives what static kinds give at that width: `○` on `u8` gives complex numbers with 32-bit parts. `⌹` and polar `∧` give fixed integers floats of the width that their division gives. A roll of fixed integers gives fixed integers, and a bound of 0, which rolls a float, is a DOMAIN error.

```bpl
⍳3ₓ₁            ⍝ [0 1 2]ₓ₁
2ₓ⊥(9⍴1ₓ)ₓ₁     ⍝ 255ₓ₁
[0 1]ₓ₁,9ₓ      ⍝ [0 1 9]ₓ₁
⍸[0 1 1]ₓ₁      ⍝ [1 2]ₓ
```

`⍳256ₓ₁` fails, because the literal `256ₓ₁` doesn't fit `u8`. `⍳ₓ₁ 256ₓ` gives 0 to 255 as `u8`.

Fixed integer literals must fit their type. After a value, a sized suffix converts to that type. Integer narrowing wraps. Float and rational conversion floors, as `⌊` does, then clamps to the target range. NaN converts to zero; infinities convert to the range's bounds. Typed empty vectors use the same suffix, as in `⍬ₓ₁`.

Plain `ₓ` makes a fixed integer ordinary. The result is strong. Under dynamic kinds it shares the array's data without copying, and its arithmetic is then exact. Under static kinds it converts the array to the `int` width, the type of every ordinary integer there.

Reductions retain the promoted fixed type. A suffix on a function converts its result after computation. To widen the accumulator itself, use a [typed reduction seed](glyphs/slash.qmd). [Superscripts and subscripts](scripts.ipynb#subscripts) covers the suffix syntax.

## Float widths

Floats come in three widths: 64, 32 and 16 bits. `•storage` gives their kind as `"float64"`, `"float32"` and `"float16"`. [`•float`](system/float.qmd) converts an array to any of them. A 64-bit float holds about 16 significant digits, a 32-bit float about 7 and a 16-bit float about 3. They take 8, 4 and 2 bytes. The largest finite 16-bit float is 65504.

Bare numbers are floats of the default width: 64 bits under dynamic kinds and 32 under [static kinds](#static-kinds), until [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) `["float":16]`, `["float":32]` or `["float":64]` sets one width for both. Code parsed after the change reads its numbers at the new width. In a REPL or a notebook, that is the next input. Leading `•prefs` calls on a literal record run before the rest of their code is parsed. A script, a notebook cell, a module or `⍎` text that starts with `•prefs ["float":32]` therefore reads its own numbers at 32 bits. Numbers that `•csv`, `•json` and `•vfi` read also take the default width. So do random numbers, the numbers that `•image` reads, and floats that a function gives from exact arguments, such as `√2ₓ`. Times from `•time` and `•date` are always 64-bit, because a 32-bit float holds seconds since 1970 only to within about two minutes. `ₕ` marks a 16-bit float, `ₛ` a 32-bit float and `ₚ` a 64-bit float, whatever the default. Display marks floats of the other widths, once after an array's notation. `•literal⁻¹` marks every float. Its text therefore reads back the same at any default.

```bpl
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[1.5ₕ 1.5ₛ [1.5 2.5]ₚ ⍬ₛ]       ⍝ "float16" "float32" "float64" "float32"
[1.5 2.5]ₛ                          ⍝ [1.5 2.5]ₛ
•literal⁻¹ 0.5                     ⍝ "0.5ₚ"
```

An operation on floats computes at their width. An exact operand rounds to the width that the operation computes at. Floats of two widths compute at the wider, except that a [weak number](#weak-and-strong-numbers) takes the width of the floats beside it. Writes, catenation and arrays built from items follow the same rule: `v,2.5`, `v.[0]←2.5` and `[v₀ 2.5]` keep a 32-bit `v`'s width. No operation widens floats on its own.

```bpl
v←32 •float 1.5 2.5
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[v×2ₓ v×v *v v×2 v×2ₚ v×v₀ v,2.5 [v₀ 2.5]]       ⍝ "float32" "float32" "float32" "float32" "float64" "float32" "float32" "float32"
•float v                     ⍝ 32ₓ
32•float1.5 × 16777217ₓ    ⍝ 25165824
```

Complex numbers have 64-bit or 32-bit parts. `•storage` gives their kind as `"complex128"` and `"complex64"`, after their whole size. They follow the rules for floats. A complex number takes the width of the floats it comes from, and a 16-bit float that becomes complex takes 32-bit parts. A complex number beside a float computes at the wider of their widths. A complex result with no imaginary part is a float of its parts' width. `ₛ`, `ₚ` and `ₕ` mark the width of the parts, and display marks parts that aren't of the default width:

```bpl
⊢.kind¨•storage¨[[2j3]ₛ;[2j3]ₕ;√[¯4]ₛ;[2j3]ₛ×1.5]       ⍝ "complex64" "complex64" "complex64" "complex64"
√¯4ₛ                                       ⍝ 0j2ₛ
```

Each operation on 16-bit floats computes in 32 bits and rounds its result to 16 bits. For `+ - × ÷` and `√`, that gives the result of 16-bit arithmetic. Folds, scans and inner products keep their running totals in 32 bits. Only their results round to 16 bits. A 16-bit total of these numbers would stop growing at 256:

```bpl
+/ 16•float4096⍴0.1   ⍝ 409.5ₕ
```

An exact operand converts straight to 32 bits, not to 16. A count larger than 65,504, the largest 16-bit float, still divides a 16-bit sum:

```bpl
h←16 •float 100000⍴1 0
+/÷≢ h                   ⍝ 0.49975586ₕ
```

[Power](glyphs/star-diaeresis.qmd) `⍣∞` stops at two results within relative tolerance `1E¯14` of each other, or within 4 units in the last place for 16-bit and 32-bit results. See [Mathish mode](#mathish-mode) for comparison and division rules.

## Accuracy

Pervasive functions on floats, such as `÷`, `*`, `⍟` and `○`, give results within 4 units in the last place of the correctly rounded result. Rustymath's [Accuracy page](https://answerdotai.github.io/rustymath/accuracy.html) lists the exceptions.

Some results are exact. Powers, roots and cube roots whose exact result is a float give it exactly. A logarithm to base 2 or 10 is exact at a power of its base. `○y`, and `*` of a complex number whose imaginary part is `y`, give an exact direction where `y` is the float nearest a whole number of quarter turns, up to 256 of them. `○π0.5` is then exactly `0j1`. With Mathish mode off, as in these examples, `=` is exact:

```bpl
•prefs ["mathish":$f]
7*5 = 16807          ⍝ $t
3√27 = 3             ⍝ $t
10⍟1000 = 3          ⍝ $t
○π0.5 = 0j1          ⍝ $t
•prefs ["mathish":$t]
```

Last bits aren't reproducible. A calculation can give results that differ in their last bits on another platform or build, in another run, with another number of threads, at another array size, or by another route, such as one fused loop in place of separate calls. `+/` adds in an order that depends on the array's size, the number of threads and the route. `⌈` and `⌊` can give either argument where one is NaN or both are zeros of opposite signs. Compare floats from different routes within a tolerance, as Mathish mode's `=` does.

## Mathish mode

[Mathish mode](mathish.qmd) is on by default. For [Mathish types](terms.qmd#term-mathish-types), floating comparisons use relative tolerance `1E¯14`, measured against the larger magnitude, and `0÷0` and `1⍟1` give zero. Disable it with `•prefs ["mathish":$f]` for exact floating comparisons and NaN at floating zero divided by zero.

The calculation's kind and `kinds` setting decide whether these conventions apply. Explicit 64-bit float suffixes and imported buffers follow the same rule as literals. Static calculations and fixed-integer operations never use Mathish conventions, even when their floating computation uses 64 bits. The narrower floats keep exact comparisons and raw division. Acceptance of integer and Boolean arguments and convergence stopping rules are independent of Mathish mode.

## Infinities and NaN

Floats include `∞`, `¯∞`, NaN and `¯0` besides finite numbers. An undefined result is NaN rather than an error, except for Mathish mode's zero divided by zero. `1÷0` is `∞`, and `⍟0` is `¯∞`. NaN is written `$n`:

```bpl
[0÷0 ∞-∞]            ⍝ 0 $n
[1÷0 ⍟0]             ⍝ ∞ ¯∞
```

Under `=`, NaN equals nothing, as in IEEE. `≡`, search, grade and Key treat NaN as one value, and grade puts it after every other number:

```bpl
$n=$n                ⍝ $f
$n≡$n                ⍝ $t
```

Complex arithmetic follows the `num_complex` crate. A complex number can have infinite or NaN parts.

An infinity or NaN is a float. Joining one to exact integers makes them floats, as any float does:

```bpl
⍳3ₓ , ∞              ⍝ 0 1 2 ∞
(•storage ⍳3ₓ , ∞).kind   ⍝ "float64"
```

CSV and JSON imports give NaN for a missing number. An integer column with gaps then becomes floats. A column that also holds an integer too large for a float to hold exactly keeps each item's kind, in mixed storage.

`⌊` and `⌈` return an exact argument unchanged beside an infinity:

```bpl
3ₓ⌊∞                 ⍝ 3ₓ
```

The [`⌈`](glyphs/upstile.qmd) and [`⌊`](glyphs/downstile.qmd) pages give their results beside NaN. Arithmetic with an infinity gives floats.

## Static kinds

Some functions choose a result's kind from their arguments' values. `√¯4` is complex because the argument is negative, `1j0` is a float because its imaginary part is zero, and an exact integer that overflows grows. Under [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) `["kinds":"static"]`, a result's kind follows from the function and its arguments' kinds alone. A fused computation needs that, because it decides each result's kind before it runs. Real arguments give real results, with NaN outside a function's domain, and complex results stay complex. `⌊`, `⌈` and monadic `×` of floats give floats, and integer `÷` gives floats. With `ₓ` after them they give integers, as Rust's `as` converts a float: NaN gives 0, and a value past the `int` width's range gives its largest or smallest integer:

```bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
√¯4 9                ⍝ $n 3
0j1×0j1              ⍝ ¯1ⱼ0
⌊2.5 ∞               ⍝ 2 ∞
7ₓ÷2ₓ                ⍝ 3.5
⌊ₓ2.5 ¯2.5           ⍝ [2 ¯3]ₓ
7ₓ÷ₓ2ₓ               ⍝ 3ₓ
⌊ₓ $n ∞              ⍝ [0 2147483647]ₓ
0÷0                  ⍝ $n
0.7=0.1+0.6          ⍝ $f
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

Ordinary integers compute at the width that the `int` pref sets, 32 bits by default, or at a wider integer's width, and wrap where a result doesn't fit. An ordinary integer is a fixed integer of the `int` width. Display marks a fixed integer of that width with plain `ₓ`. Their storage takes that width too, whatever their values. Code that wants narrow storage writes a fixed type, such as `ₓ₁`. New floats take 32 bits, unless the `float` pref sets a width. Fixed integers retain their explicit type. An integer beside a float takes the float's width. A weak number beside floats takes their width, as under dynamic kinds. Exact fractions stay exact. `⌹` and polar `∧` give integers floats of the width that `÷` gives them. A roll of integers gives integers, and a bound of 0, which rolls a float, is a DOMAIN error. Floating comparisons are exact. An ordinary integer literal that doesn't fit the `int` width is a LIMIT error. [`•csv`](system/csv.qmd) and [`•json`](system/json.qmd) read integers at the `int` width too, and their `types` option gives a column another type:

```bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
2147483647ₓ+1ₓ             ⍝ ¯2147483648ₓ
[1 2]ₓ₄+1ₓ                 ⍝ [2 3]ₓ
(•memory ⍳100ₓ).bytes      ⍝ 400ₓ
(•memory ⍳100ₓ₁).bytes     ⍝ 100ₓ
(•storage (32•float1 2)×2ₚ).kind    ⍝ "float64"
(•storage (32•float1 2)×2ₓ).kind    ⍝ "float32"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

[Performance](performance.qmd) explains why static kinds are the setting for performance work. Code for static kinds gives each integer the width that its values need and gives `•csv` and `•json` a `types` record for their columns. Code written for dynamic kinds can give other results. Dynamic kinds give this total of positions exactly. Static kinds wrap it at the 32-bit range, unless a 64-bit seed widens the sum:

```bpl
+/⍳100000ₓ                 ⍝ 4999950000ₓ
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
+/⍳100000ₓ                 ⍝ 704982704ₓ
0ₓ₈+/⍳100000ₓ              ⍝ 4999950000ₓ₈
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

Under static kinds, a write whose items have another kind converts the whole array to the compact type that holds both kinds, where one exists. The array's type then doesn't depend on which items the write selects. Under dynamic kinds, each written item keeps its own kind in mixed storage:

```bpl
v←[1 2 3]ₓ₁ ⋄ v.[[1]]←0.5 ⋄ (•storage v).kind    ⍝ "mixed"
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
v←[1 2 3]ₓ₁ ⋄ v.[[1]]←0.5 ⋄ (•storage v).kind    ⍝ "float32"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

## Booleans

Comparisons give Booleans. So does every function whose result is a truth value, such as `~`, `∊`, `⍷` and `≡`. `$t` is true and `$f` is false:

```bpl
x←3 1 4 1 5
x>2                  ⍝ $t $f $t $f $t
```

Wherever a number is expected, `$t` is 1 and `$f` is 0. `+/` counts the true items, `#` keeps the items a Boolean mask marks, and a Boolean used as an index selects position 0 or 1:

```bpl
x←3 1 4 1 5
+/x>2                ⍝ 3ₓ
x>2 # x              ⍝ 3 4 5
4>2 ⌷ "no" "yes"     ⍝ "yes"
```

A float used as a Boolean follows the [integer-acceptance rule](#exact-and-approximate) for 0 or 1.

Arithmetic on Booleans gives integers. `∧`, `∨`, `⊽`, `⊼`, `⌊` and `⌈` on two Booleans give a Boolean:

```bpl
$t+$t                ⍝ 2ₓ
$t∧$f                ⍝ $f
```

Boolean storage takes one byte for each item. Boxed display marks it with `$`:

```bpl
(•storage $t $f).kind   ⍝ "bool"
```
